# Abstract

Operation Viscount Project CENTAUR-II reconstructs the long-run demographic series of the Central Plains (USGS Hydrological Unit 11, Arkansas-White-Red drainage, 645.289 km² across 9.311 five-arcminute cells) from 10000BC to 1600AD.

Combining 143 catalogued archaeological settlements (376 dated benchmark observations across 298 ledger candidates) with continuous rural priors interpolated from the continental North American non-stationary Matérn composite (93.129 unique site-periods across 3.833 domestic catchments, 2.570 active, and 251 cross-frontier buffers, a 14,24x baseline multiplier over the 6.539 legacy global radiocarbon baseline), total population rises from 1.000 in 10000BC to 86,3k at 0AD and peaks at 160k (147,2k to 172,8k; 0,248 persons per km²) in 1500AD.

Guided by Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] HU 11 summed radiocarbon curve (N = 1.549 terrestrial dates, median peak 1483AD, 467 cal BP), sub-regional maxima diverge sharply in timing. The Lower Arkansas and Red River Caddoan zone peaked at 1300AD (58,5k) around Spiro and related mound centres before easing to 52k in 1500AD, whereas the Middle Arkansas Wichita prairies (72k) and High Plains (36k) continued growing through 1500AD.

Following mid-sixteenth-century Spanish expeditions and Old World epidemic spread along Southern Plains exchange routes, regional population declined by 21,88% from 1500AD to 125k (115k to 135k; 0,194 persons per km²) in 1600AD [@vehik2002wichita; @perttula1992caddo; @jones2014].

# Background

## Prairie Gradient and Earlier Continental Limitations

Earlier continental population atlases smoothed indigenous North American density across broad longitudinal zones or fixed post-contact multiplication ratios, flattening the pronounced moisture and agrarian gradient spanning USGS Hydrological Unit 11 [@ubelaker2006; @milner2010]. Across these 645,29k km² of the Arkansas, Canadian, Cimarron, White and upper Red river drainages, mean precipitation triples from semi-arid Llano Estacado shortgrass steppe in the west to humid Ozark and Ouachita oak-hickory lowlands in the east.

Archaeological records across this transect establish three distinct demographic regimes rather than a uniform bison-nomad hinterland. Along the Lower Arkansas, White and Red River Great Bend, Woodland mound builders at Toltec Mounds gave way after 950AD to ranked Caddoan and Mississippian chiefdoms anchored at Spiro, Harlan, Crenshaw, Battle Mound and Carden Bottoms [@rolingson1998toltec; @brown1996spiro; @perttula1992caddo].

Across central Oklahoma, Kansas and the Canadian breaks, Plains Village horticulturalists along the Washita, Canadian and middle Arkansas valleys constructed semi-sedentary grass-and-thatch hamlets that coalesced during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries into populous Wichita towns such as Etzanoa and Tobias-Quivira [@drass1997washita; @wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita]. On the western Canadian and High Plains caprock, Antelope Creek-Alibates flint quarries and stone-slab farmsteads pulsed with Southern Plains maize cultivation between 1200AD and 1500AD before drought contraction returned much of the shortgrass steppe to specialised bison hunting [@lintz1986antelope].

## Radiocarbon Timing Across HU 11

Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] demonstrated that HU 11 did not experience a uniform demographic collapse contemporaneous with the American Bottom around 1150 to 1250AD. Instead, N = 1.549 screened terrestrial radiocarbon dates across the Arkansas-White-Red drainage generate a summed probability peak at 467 cal BP (1483AD, interquartile range 436 to 484 cal BP).

This late fifteenth-century basin-wide crest reconciles apparent contradictions in the regional archaeological record. Although monumental burial ceremonialism at Spiro peaked around 1300 to 1350AD and Lower Arkansas mound building ebbed during the fifteenth century [@brown1996spiro], demographic weight shifted northward and westward into coalescent Wichita farming aggregations across the Arkansas-Walnut and Little Arkansas confluences [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita].

## Climate Shocks, Geoarchaeology and Palaeoecological Benchmarks

Separating climatic contraction from archaeological visibility loss requires regional geoarchaeological benchmarks across the Central Plains and adjacent western valleys. On the western plains margin, Late Pleistocene horse tooth morphology and ancient DNA establish the ecological baseline of megafaunal turnover prior to Holocene bison-hunting intensification [@barronortiz2017cheek], while Washita and Antelope Creek faunal and architectural series trace how sedentary villagers balanced maize cropping with persistent bison procurement [@drass1997washita; @lintz1986antelope].

Deeply aggrading Holocene alluvial terraces in Kansas and Oklahoma floodplains continually bury Early and Middle Holocene occupations relative to deflated High Plains blowouts, as documented across Cross Creek, Douglass Lake, Milford Lake and Melvern Lake archaeological surveys [@defense1995dtic_ada_eea; @defense1988dtic_ada_498; @defense1995dtic_ada_f71; @defense1995dtic_ada_790]. Explicit spatial priors calibrated to local hydrography and valley terraces help correct this geomorphic burial bias.

## Ecological Zonation Between Shortgrass Steppe and Ouachita Woodlands

Hydrological Unit 11 encompasses nearly seven degrees of latitude (31,73 N to 38,68 N) and more than fourteen degrees of longitude (90,51 W to 104,58 W). Precipitation increases steadily from semi-arid New Mexico and Texas caprock breaks toward humid Arkansas lowlands, creating sharp gradients in frost-free growing seasons and timber cover.

That moisture gradient separated western caprock communities, where dry-farmed plots faced recurring drought risk around 1350 to 1450AD, from eastern river valleys buffered by oak mast, fish-bearing oxbow lakes and alluvial bottomlands [@brown1996spiro; @lintz1986antelope]. Any uniform steppe density multiplier obscures this split.

Accounting simultaneously for valley-floor aggregation and upland hunting range requires integrating site-specific town chronologies with spatially continuous radiocarbon priors tuned to local hydrography.

# Methodology

## Sub-Regional Partition and Areal Masks

CENTAUR-II partitions HU 11 (9.311 five-arcminute active cells, 645.289 km², spanning 31,73 N to 38,68 N and 90,51 W to 104,58 W) into three hydrological and ecological sub-regions (Table \ref{tab:cp-structure}):

1. **Upper Arkansas, Cimarron and Llano Estacado High Plains** (176.205 km², 27,31%, 2.550 cells, 8 catalogued sites): encompasses southeastern Colorado, northeastern New Mexico, western Kansas and the western panhandle breaks, including Palaeoindian bison kills (Folsom, Olsen-Chubbuck, Winger), upland camps and stone enclosures (Chalk Hollow, Sopris, Cramer, Bell) and the protohistoric Edwards I Fortified Village [@lintz1986antelope].
2. **Middle Arkansas, Neosho-Grand, Canadian and Washita Prairies** (299.859 km², 46,47%, 4.345 cells, 103 catalogued sites): covers central Kansas, Oklahoma and the Canadian River Panhandle breaks, capturing early bison kills (Miami, Cooper Bison Kill, Lipscomb), caprock Plains Village stone-slab clusters (Antelope Creek-Alibates, Buried City), Washita River hamlets (Washita-Duncan) and coalescent Wichita towns (Etzanoa, Tobias-Quivira, Tobias Great Bend Town, Spanish Fort Taovaya Town, Longest Wichita Town, Little River and Deer Creek) [@drass1997washita; @wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita; @lintz1986antelope].
3. **Lower Arkansas Valley, Ozark Fringe and Red River Bend** (169.225 km², 26,22%, 2.416 cells, 32 catalogued sites): integrates eastern Oklahoma, western and central Arkansas, southwestern Missouri and adjacent Red River counties anchored by Toltec Mounds, Spiro, Harlan, Crenshaw, Battle Mound, Battle Mound Caddo City, Hatchel, Roitsch and Carden Bottoms [@rolingson1998toltec; @brown1996spiro; @perttula1992caddo].

```{r tbl-structure, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod$regions)
sett_vals <- unname(sett_data)
df_struct <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(reg_keys), function(i) {
  rk <- reg_keys[i]
  rv <- mod$regions[[rk]]
  sub_sites <- Filter(function(s) identical(s$region_id, rk), sett_vals)
  pops <- unlist(rv$population)
  pk <- max(as.numeric(pops))
  pk_yr <- names(pops)[which.max(as.numeric(pops))]
  pk_lbl <- if (as.integer(pk_yr) < 0) paste0(abs(as.integer(pk_yr)), "BC") else paste0(pk_yr, "AD")
  short_nm <- c(
    "1. High Plains and Upper Ark.",
    "2. Middle Ark. and Washita",
    "3. Lower Ark. and Spiro"
  )[i]
  data.frame(
    SubRegion = short_nm,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(rv$area_km2, 0L),
    Share = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * rv$area_km2 / mod$total_area_km2, 2L), "%"),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_sites)),
    PeakPop = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk), " (", pk_lbl, ")"),
    PeakDens = viscount_fmt_number(pk / rv$area_km2, 3L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
rownames(df_struct) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_struct,
  "Sub-regional areal geometry, catalogued settlement counts and peak demographic densities in the Central Plains (HU 11).",
  c("Sub-region", "Area (km²)", "Area Share", "Sites", "Peak (Year)", "Peak Density (per km²)"),
  list(label = "tab:cp-structure", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Multi-Registry Radiocarbon Kriging and Benchmark Calibration

Rural habitation weights across HU 11 derive from the continental North American non-stationary Matérn composite, which harmonises p3k14c [@bird2022p3k14c], c14bazAAR, state site-file registries [@kelly2025], CRM inventories and CENTAUR monument records into 93.129 unique site-period observations across 3.833 domestic Voronoi catchments (15,52M km²; 2.570 active inhabited catchments, or 67,05%; equivalent circular radius median 29,48 km across all catchments and 29,3 km across active catchments, with 90th percentile 40,95 km and 39,85 km respectively) plus 251 cross-frontier buffer catchments across 493.687 valid terrestrial five-arcminute cells (18,56M km²).

This composite offers a 14,24x spatial observation multiplier over the 6.539-record legacy global radiocarbon baseline. Site densities are transformed via Freeman-Tukey variance stabilisation, macro-tile log-variance regularisation and 1-ring Poisson-Gamma credibility shrinkage before weighted least-squares (WLS) covariate regression and non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging [@paciorek2006matern], activating 78.938 to 149.138 non-wasteland cells across ten Holocene horizons.

Biophysical covariates capture steep prairie aridity gradients using 13,5 km fluvial distance decay, exponential coastal proximity, terrain slope and habitable cell fraction. Radiocarbon phase calibration [@crema2021rcarbon] alongside regional reservoir surveys at Milford Lake and Big Hill Lake [@defense1995dtic_ada_f71; @defense1980dtic_ada_623; @remsburg1919anoldkan_7934ec] supports treating dated habitation intensity strictly as relative rural suitability rather than raw per-capita headcounts.

## Temporal Horizon Interpolation and Frontier Smoothing

Whereas HU 11 tabulates 23 demographic benchmarks between 10000BC and 1600AD, the continental kriging framework constructs non-stationary surfaces across ten canonical Holocene horizons spanning 13000BC to 1650AD (13000 to 6000BC, 6000 to 3000BC, 3000 to 1000BC, 1000 to 200BC, 200BC to 400AD, 400 to 800AD, 800 to 1100AD, 1100 to 1300AD, 1300 to 1500AD and 1500 to 1650AD). Intermediate Woodland and sixteenth-century intervals receive linearly blended spatial weight surfaces normalised within each sub-regional mask.

Cross-frontier 300 km buffer catchments bridge HU 11 smoothly across artificial hydrological borders: westward into Rio Grande and Pecos tributaries, northward into Platte-Republican Central Plains sites, and eastward along the Ouachita, Red and Mississippi bottomlands toward HU 08 and HU 07.

## Urban Subtraction and Uncertainty Intervals

For each sub-region $r$ and benchmark horizon $t \in \{-10000, \dots, 1600\}$, catalogued town populations summed across all 143 included sites in the settlement gazetteer are subtracted from sub-regional targets $P_r(t)$ prior to rural allocation:

$$R_r(t) = P_r(t) - \sum_{i \in S_r} U_i(t), \qquad R_r(t) \ge 0$$

Rural residuals $R_r(t)$ distribute proportionally across active five-arcminute cells according to the interpolated North American Matérn weights and undergo two separable 5-pixel smoothing passes. Symmetric 8 per cent interval bounds (plus or minus 8 per cent around regional totals) reflect alluvial site-burial uncertainty and sixteenth-century Spanish eyewitness league variance across dispersed Wichita grass-lodge compounds [@wedel1982quivira].

# Testing and Validation

Five verification gates pass with zero errors as of 18 November 2026 GMT+0:

1. **Radiocarbon Sample Threshold**: HU 11 rests on N = 1.549 terrestrial radiocarbon dates [@kelly2025], nearly four times the 400-date reliability floor required for two-millennium peak estimation [@crema2021rcarbon].
2. **Non-Stationary Kriging Sharpness**: Across all ten horizons (13000BC to 1650AD) of the North American composite, the Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) variogram satisfies regularised $\tau_1 = 1,35$ on all ten horizons (unregularised 1,519 to 1,6098, mean 1,5782), $\tau_2 = 2,9025$ (2,9), effective short range 45,23 km to 47,94 km (mean 47,00 km), unregularised raw nugget 0 across all ten horizons, regularised nugget-to-sill ratio 0,04 across all ten horizons (below 0,45), and WLS fit $R^2$ from 0,9990 to 0,9992.
3. **Gazetteer and Ledger Reconciliation**: Cross-checking the 143 included settlements (376 dated observations, averaging 2,63 per site with 62 holding three or more benchmarks, spanning 31,73 to 38,68 N and 90,51 to 104,58 W: 8 in High Plains, 103 in Middle Arkansas and 32 in Lower Arkansas) against 298 source-ledger candidates (155 excluded: 154 duplicate-alias consolidations merged within 2 km of canonical sites plus one non-habitation rockshelter at Sliding Slab Rock Shelter) leaves zero unmatched keys and zero coordinate errors.
4. **Urban-Rural Mass Conservation**: Direct benchmark-dated settlement sums stay strictly within sub-regional targets at every benchmark, growing from 95 of 4.250 inhabitants (2,24%) at 8000BC and 830 (0,69%) at 600AD to 8.880 (5,79% of 153,5k) in 1200AD, 14.750 (9,32% of 158,2k) in 1300AD, 19.620 (12,26% of 160k) in 1500AD, 33.310 (23,38% of 142,5k) in 1550AD and 33.340 (26,67% of 125k) in 1600AD.
5. **Arithmetic Benchmark Consistency**: Sub-regional series and 8 per cent uncertainty intervals sum identically to the headline basin series across all 23 horizons (10000BC to 1600AD).

```{r tbl-subregions, results='asis'}

  ),
```

# Results

## Palaeoindian Bison Kill Horizons and Archaic Prairie Expansion

Following retreat of Pleistocene ice sheets and megafaunal turnover across western valleys, early Holocene archaeology across HU 11 anchors one of the continent's oldest documented bison-procurement landscapes.

Palaeoindian camps and kill sites along the Llano Estacado, Texas Panhandle and Southern High Plains margins (including Miami from 9500 to 9200BC, Cooper Bison Kill from 9200 to 8400BC and Lipscomb from 8900 to 8600BC on the eastern panhandle breaks, alongside Folsom from 8700 to 8300BC, Olsen-Chubbuck from 8300 to 7100BC and Winger from 7100 to 6600BC in the Upper Arkansas High Plains) register small mobile bands (30 to 75 people per aggregation) harvesting late glacial *Bison antiquus* herds [@barronortiz2017cheek].

Total HU 11 population grew slowly from 1.000 (920 to 1.080; 0,002 persons per km²) in 10000BC and 4.250 (3.910 to 4.590) in 8000BC to 19,6k in 5000BC, 39,4k in 3000BC and 52,7k in 2000BC.

Archaic prairie camps such as William Young (4800 to 1200BC) exploited gallery forests, spring-fed bison wallows and Alibates chert outcrops across both mixed prairies and Ozark uplands. Broad-spectrum plant processing, nut harvesting and deer hunting supported slow, continuous growth across 3000 to 1000BC (39,4k up to 68,3k) ahead of pottery introduction.

By 0AD, regional population stood at 86,3k (79,4k to 93,2k; 0,134 persons per km²), with 33k (38,24%) residing in the humid Lower Arkansas and Red River lowlands against 31,5k (36,5%) on the Middle Arkansas prairies and 21,8k (25,26%) across the semi-arid High Plains (Figure \ref{fig:traj-central-plains}).

```{r fig-traj, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_central_plains_trajectory.png",
  "Total and sub-regional population trajectory in the Central Plains (HU 11) with uncertainty interval, 10000BC to 1600AD.",
  "fig:traj-central-plains"
)
```

## Woodland Ceremonial Centres and Caddoan Mound Climax

Across the Middle and Late Woodland (200 to 1000AD), regional totals rose steadily from 97,5k in 200AD to 120,7k in 600AD, 132k in 800AD and 141,4k in 1000AD. In the Lower Arkansas Valley, Plum Bayou earthwork planners raised sixteen-mound civic-ceremonial complexes led by Toltec Mounds (1.450 at 800AD, active 600 to 1000AD), establishing fixed floodplain ritual capitals well ahead of Mississippian shell-tempered pottery [@rolingson1998toltec].

Between 950AD and 1350AD, Caddoan ceremonial polities reshaped the eastern third of HU 11 and adjacent Neosho margins. Harlan (980 at 1100AD) and Crenshaw (980 at 1150AD) alongside Norman (740 at 1150AD) transitioned into the premier regional necropolis at Spiro (3.100 at 1350AD, active 900 to 1450AD), paired southward along the Red River Great Bend with Battle Mound (1.650 at 1400AD), Battle Mound Caddo City (1.300 at 1500AD), Hatchel (1.100 at 1450AD), Roitsch (920 at 1400AD) and Belcher (780 at 1400AD) [@brown1996spiro; @perttula1992caddo].

Driven by Caddoan intensification, the Lower Arkansas-Spiro sub-region attained its Holocene peak of 58,5k (53,8k to 63,2k; 0,346 persons per km², 36,98% of HU 11) in 1300AD, two centuries before western prairie and High Plains trajectories topped out (Table \ref{tab:cp-subregions}).

## Prairie Coalescence, High Plains Expansion and Sixteenth-Century Shift

While Caddoan mound construction waned after 1400AD (55k in 1400AD down to 52k in 1500AD), demographic growth accelerated across the Middle Arkansas prairies and Washita-Canadian basins [@drass1997washita; @vehik2002wichita]. Middle Arkansas population rose from 55,5k in 1000AD to 65,5k in 1300AD, 69k in 1400AD and a sub-regional peak of 72k (66,2k to 77,8k; 0,24 persons per km², 45% of HU 11) in 1500AD (Figure \ref{fig:shares-central-plains}).

On the Canadian River caprock breaks, Plains Village farmsteads around Antelope Creek-Alibates (1.200 at 1300AD, anchored near quarry sources occupied intermittently since 8000BC) and Buried City (680 at 1300AD) expanded maize-and-bison storage economies before fifteenth-century drought thinned stone-slab hamlets [@lintz1986antelope]. Further west on the High Plains, Sopris (320 at 1050AD), Cramer (240 at 1250AD), Bell (210 at 1180AD) and late bison-hunting bands pushed the Upper Arkansas division to a 36k peak (0,204 persons per km²) in 1500AD, lifting HU 11 as a whole to its Holocene maximum of 160k (147,2k to 172,8k; 0,248 persons per km²) in 1500AD, closely matching the 1483AD Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] radiocarbon peak.

This divergence highlights the east-west hydraulic asymmetry of the basin: Caddoan ceremonial towns in humid eastern valleys consolidated and devolved early, whereas tallgrass prairie villages expanded along alluvial floodplains capable of anchoring both bison procurement and reliable garden plots.

```{r fig-shares, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig3_central_plains_shares.png",
  "Sub-regional demographic composition across the Central Plains (HU 11) from 10000BC to 1600AD.",
  "fig:shares-central-plains"
)
```

In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, dispersed Wichita hamlets consolidated along the Arkansas-Walnut, Little Arkansas and Red River corridors for mutual defence against encroaching equestrian-era precursors and neighbouring Plains raiders [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita]. Coalescent towns ballooned even as rural peripheries thinned: Etzanoa (37,06 N, 97 W) reached 14k by 1600AD, joined by Tobias-Quivira (3.600 at 1550AD), Tobias Great Bend Town (2.000), Spanish Fort Taovaya Town (1.500), Tobias (1.400), Longest Wichita Town (1.200), Little River (1.180) and Malone (1.100) (Table \ref{tab:cp-top-sites}).

Consequently, Middle Arkansas's direct benchmark-dated urbanised share surged from 12,95% (8.480 of 65,5k) in 1300AD and 19,93% (14.350 of 72k) in 1500AD to 52,7% (30.040 of 57k) in 1600AD. Following Coronado's 1541AD entrada and Oñate's 1601AD encounter, Old World pathogens and bison-trade warfare reduced HU 11 from 160k in 1500AD to 142,5k in 1550AD and 125k (0,194 persons per km²) in 1600AD (21,88% decline) [@ubelaker2006; @jones2014; @milner2010].

```{r tbl-top-sites, results='asis'}
sett_list <- unname(sett_data)
reg_short <- c(
  cp_high_plains_upper_arkansas = "High Plains",
  cp_neosho_verdigris_washita_prairies = "Middle Arkansas",
  cp_arkansas_valley_ozark_spiro = "Lower Ark.-Spiro"
)
pk_nums <- vapply(sett_list, function(s) max(unlist(s$population)), numeric(1))
ord <- order(pk_nums, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(10L, length(ord))
top_sites <- sett_list[ord[seq_len(top_n)]]
df_top <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(top_sites), function(i) {
  s <- top_sites[[i]]
  pops <- unlist(s$population)
  yrs <- as.integer(names(pops))
  pk <- max(as.numeric(pops))
  pk_y <- yrs[which.max(as.numeric(pops))]
  pk_lbl <- if (pk_y < 0) paste0(abs(pk_y), "BC") else paste0(pk_y, "AD")
  data.frame(
    Rank = as.character(i),
    Site = clean_text(s$name),
    SubRegion = reg_short[[s$region_id]],
    Peak = viscount_fmt_pop(pk),
    Year = pk_lbl,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
rownames(df_top) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Top ten catalogued settlements by peak population in the Central Plains (HU 11).",
  c("Rank", "Settlement", "Sub-region", "Peak Pop.", "Peak Year"),
  list(label = "tab:cp-top-sites", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Settlement Primacy and Urban-Rural Balance

Across all 143 catalogued settlements in HU 11, rank-size hierarchy shifted dramatically between 1300AD and 1600AD. During the Caddoan climax, major eastern centres (Spiro at 3.100 in 1350AD, Battle Mound at 1.650 in 1400AD, Hatchel at 1.100 in 1450AD) anchored a wider mound network alongside Panhandle caprock farmsteads (Antelope Creek-Alibates 1.200, Buried City 680), while direct benchmark-dated entries summed to 14.750 (9,32% of 158,2k) across the basin in 1300AD.

By 1600AD, coalescence into fortified Wichita macro-towns along the Arkansas-Walnut and Red River corridors lifted direct benchmark-dated urbanised population to 33.340 (26,67% of 125k), even while Panhandle caprock stone-slab settlements contracted sharply after 1500AD, leaving Edwards I Fortified Village (550 at 1600AD) as the sole quantified High Plains centre.

That spatial shift demonstrates how regional population stability near the eastern prairie ecotone masked acute western contraction after 1450AD. Between 1300AD and 1600AD, the centre of urban gravity shifted nearly 400 km northwestward from the Arkansas Valley into the middle Arkansas plains.

This geographic migration reconciles earlier archaeological syntheses that treated eastern Caddoan depopulation as basin-wide abandonment [@brown1996spiro; @vehik2002wichita]. Even as monumental mound precincts closed in Arkansas and eastern Oklahoma, aggregated Wichita settlements absorbed high regional densities further upstream.

## Sub-Regional Trajectories Across the Three Tiers

### Upper Arkansas, Cimarron and Llano Estacado High Plains

Spanning 176.205 km² (27,31% of HU 11), the western caprock grew from 350 inhabitants (322 to 378) in 10000BC to 5,9k in 5000BC and 21,8k (0,124 persons per km²) by 0AD. Mobile Archaic bison-hunting bands depended on canyon springs, playa lakes and upland stone shelters across southeastern Colorado, northeastern New Mexico and western Kansas [@lintz1986antelope; @barronortiz2017cheek].

Late prehistoric expansion carried the sub-region through Sopris (320 at 1050AD), Cramer (240 at 1250AD) and Bell (210 at 1180AD) from 31,4k in 1000AD to 34,2k in 1300AD, peaking modestly at 36k (33,1k to 38,9k; 0,204 persons per km²) in 1500AD as specialised bison nomads joined protohistoric Edwards I Fortified Village (350 in 1500AD rising to 550 in 1600AD). Post-1500AD raiding and Old World contagion lowered western numbers to 33k in 1550AD and 30k (0,17 persons per km²) by 1600AD [@jones2014].

### Middle Arkansas, Neosho-Grand, Canadian and Washita Prairies

Encompassing 299.859 km² (46,47% of HU 11), central Oklahoma, Kansas and the Canadian breaks rose from 300 inhabitants in 10000BC and 6,5k in 5000BC to 31,5k (0,105 persons per km²) at 0AD and 55,5k in 1000AD. Washita River Plains Village farmers and Antelope Creek caprock towns multiplied along sandy river terraces and canyon breaks during the twelfth to fourteenth centuries (65,5k in 1300AD), pairing riverbottom maize with tallgrass bison hunts [@drass1997washita; @lintz1986antelope].

Fifteenth-century coalescence around the Great Bend of the Arkansas lifted this middle tier to a peak of 72k (66,2k to 77,8k; 0,24 persons per km², 45% of all HU 11 inhabitants) in 1500AD [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita]. Subsequent disease outbreaks following 1541AD dropped totals to 64,5k (1550AD) and 57k (0,19 persons per km²) by 1600AD, with 52,7% (30.040 of 57k) concentrated inside Etzanoa (14k), Tobias-Quivira, Tobias Great Bend Town, Spanish Fort Taovaya Town, Tobias, Longest Wichita Town, Little River and Malone.

### Lower Arkansas Valley, Ozark Fringe and Red River Bend

Across 169.225 km² (26,22% of HU 11), eastern lowland density advanced earliest, rising from 350 in 10000BC and 7,2k in 5000BC to 33k (0,195 persons per km²) by 0AD and 54,5k in 1000AD. Floodplain oxbows and oak-hickory mast supported Toltec Mounds (1.450 at 800AD), followed by Caddoan mound networks at Harlan, Crenshaw, Spiro (3.100 at 1350AD), Battle Mound (1.650 at 1400AD), Battle Mound Caddo City (1.300 at 1500AD) and Hatchel (1.100 at 1450AD) [@rolingson1998toltec; @brown1996spiro].

After reaching its sub-regional zenith of 58,5k (53,8k to 63,2k; 0,346 persons per km²) at 1300AD, the Caddoan core eased to 55k (1400AD) and 52k (1500AD) as late fourteenth-century droughts altered Arkansas Valley political integration [@perttula1992caddo]. Downstream De Soto-route epidemics (1541 to 1543AD) then accelerated contraction to 45k in 1550AD and 38k (0,225 persons per km²) in 1600AD [@ubelaker2006; @milner2010].

### Sixteenth-Century Chronicles and Regional Border Continuity

Between 1541AD and 1601AD, Coronado's and Oñate's expeditions provided first-hand league and grass-lodge enumerations across the Great Bend and Walnut River settlements while Soto's chroniclers traversed Arkansas Valley towns such as Carden Bottoms (1.450 at 1500AD) [@wedel1982quivira; @perttula1992caddo].

Across watershed divides, 300 km cross-frontier buffers inside the North American spatial framework align eastern Ozark and Red River densities continuously with HU 08 (Lower Mississippi) and HU 07 (Upper Mississippi), while damping artificial drops between the Arkansas headwaters and the Rio Grande border of HU 13.

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
hl_yrs <- c("-10000", "-8000", "-5000", "-3000", "-2000", "-1000", "0", "200", "600", "1000", "1200", "1300", "1400", "1500", "1550", "1600")
reg_keys <- names(mod$regions)
get_bound <- function(yr, idx) {
  sum(vapply(reg_keys, function(k) mod$regions[[k]]$population_bounds[[yr]][idx], numeric(1)))
}
hl_vals <- vapply(hl_yrs, function(y) mod$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[y]], numeric(1))
lo_vals <- vapply(hl_yrs, function(y) get_bound(y, 1L), numeric(1))
hi_vals <- vapply(hl_yrs, function(y) get_bound(y, 2L), numeric(1))

df_bench <- data.frame(
  Year = ifelse(as.integer(hl_yrs) < 0, paste0(abs(as.integer(hl_yrs)), "BC"), paste0(hl_yrs, "AD")),
  Total = vapply(hl_vals, viscount_fmt_pop, character(1)),
  Lower = vapply(lo_vals, viscount_fmt_pop, character(1)),
  Upper = vapply(hi_vals, viscount_fmt_pop, character(1)),
  Density = vapply(hl_vals / mod$total_area_km2, function(d) viscount_fmt_number(d, 3L), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(df_bench) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  df_bench,
  "Headline population trajectory, 8% uncertainty intervals and mean density across the Central Plains (HU 11), 10000BC to 1600AD.",
  c("Benchmark", "Total Pop.", "Lower Bound", "Upper Bound", "Density (per km²)"),
  list(label = "tab:cp-benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations

Across HU 11, archaeological preservation biases interact strongly with soil moisture and alluvial sedimentation regimes, making transparent error stratification indispensable for downstream historical syntheses.

Four evidentiary limitations qualify the HU 11 demographic series:

1. **Alluvial Floodplain Burial**: Deep Holocene meander belts and rapid overbank alluviation along the lower Arkansas, Canadian and Red rivers conceal Archaic and Early Woodland sites beneath thick alluvium, depressing recovery relative to deflated High Plains blowouts [@rolingson1998toltec; @defense1995dtic_ada_eea; @defense1995dtic_ada_790].

2. **Mobile Bison-Hunter Radiocarbon Scarcity**: Following 1450AD drought abandonment of semi-sedentary Plains Village hamlets on the western steppe, mobile bison-hunting camps generated far fewer charcoal features per capita than sedentary earthlodge or stone-slab houses [@lintz1986antelope; @drass1997washita].

3. **Spanish Entrada Headcount Variance**: Protohistoric Wichita town figures (Etzanoa, Tobias-Quivira) rely heavily on 1541AD and 1601AD Spanish chronicles whose league counts and grass-lodge tallies span wide compound areas [@wedel1982quivira; @vehik2002wichita].

4. **Cross-Border Caddoan Continuity**: Southeastern Caddoan lineages along the Red River Great Bend interacted continuously with Lower Mississippi Valley centres beyond HU 11; sub-regional estimates across the eastern Ozark-Red River boundary therefore depend on the 300 km continental smoothing buffers to avoid edge discontinuities [@perttula1992caddo].

# Conclusion

The Central Plains (HU 11) exemplifies asynchronous indigenous demographic development within a single continental watershed. Early Caddoan agricultural intensification propelled Lower Arkansas-Spiro densities to a 1300AD summit (58,5k), two centuries before the central prairies (72k) and High Plains (36k) lifted the watershed as a whole to its 160k (0,248 persons per km²) zenith around 1500AD.

Fifteenth- and sixteenth-century prairie coalescence concentrated over half of all Middle Arkansas inhabitants inside fortified Wichita river towns (30.040 of 57k in 1600AD, or 52,7%), even as early colonial contact and epidemics initiated a 21,88% regional downturn after 1500AD.

Western Canadian and caprock communities thinned permanent stone-slab settlements by 1500AD, shifting toward specialised bison-hunting economies well ahead of widespread equestrian adoption. That dual transformation explains how basin-wide demographic numbers plateaued between 1300AD and 1500AD despite acute sub-regional upheaval.

Pairing 143 settlements (376 dated observations; Table \ref{tab:cp-top-sites}) with the continental North American radiocarbon composite (93.129 unique site-periods across 3.833 domestic catchments, 2.570 active, and 493.687 terrestrial cells) captures this west-to-east ecological split while conserving basin-wide mass across every benchmark from 10000BC to 1600AD [@kelly2025; @ubelaker2006]. Future stratified alluvial cores from the Washita, Canadian and Arkansas terraces can enter the spatial prior directly without revising aggregate town totals.

More broadly, the Central Plains sequence shows how indigenous North American demography sustained regional peaks after 1400AD even as major Mississippian mound centres contracted eastward. Combining radiocarbon probability envelopes with site-level town series captures both long-term rural carrying capacity and late pre-contact urban coalescence across the Arkansas-Red drainage.
